### D-184 — T-228: the supply-chain gates land in CI — `cargo audit` beside cargo-deny, a full `pnpm audit`, and a dependency-free license allow-list check in place of the spec's `license-checker` (which sees 24 of 257 installed packages under pnpm) — 2026-11-23

Problem: SEC-010 (docs/spec.md:897) has demanded `cargo audit`,
`cargo-deny` and `npm audit` in CI since spec v1.0, and §5.3's "License
checks" row (docs/spec.md:154) names `license-checker` for the npm side;
CI ran only `cargo-deny` (the `deny` job, D-060's structure). Card T-228:
the gates as separate steps, done "when the job falls on a known
vulnerability or an incompatible license". Five questions the card left
open, each settled before the first edit (rule 1).

1. _Where the steps live: inside the existing jobs, no new job._
   `cargo audit` joins `deny`; `pnpm audit` and the license check join
   `lint`. Both are checks main's branch protection requires — read
   through the protection API on 2026-11-23: lint, test, deny, e2e,
   build × 4 legs — so each new gate blocks a merge by construction. A
   new `audit` job would report red and block nothing until someone
   added it to that list by hand. `deny` keeps its id and name (a
   rename orphans the required context — D-060's round-1 P0), the job
   count stays at fourteen, and `ci-rerun/decide.py`, which knows only
   `test` and the `test-matrix (` prefix, needs nothing.

2. _`npm audit` reads `pnpm audit`._ The toolchain has been pnpm since
   D-018; the orchestrator's ruling, D-182's follow-up. SEC-010 now
   names the real command (rule 11).

3. _The license tool: not `license-checker`._ Measured on a scratch
   copy of `package.json` + `pnpm-lock.yaml` + `pnpm-workspace.yaml`
   (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts`, pnpm 12.6.0):

   | Inventory                                                      | Packages seen                                        |
   | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
   | `pnpm licenses list --json`                                    | 257 installed versions under 246 names               |
   | `license-checker@25.0.1` (the card's and the spec's tool; dlx) | 25 — the 24 direct dependencies and the private root |
   | `license-checker-rseidelsohn@5.0.1` (the maintained fork)      | 252 — all but the five platform binaries             |

   The five the fork misses: `@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu`,
   `@tailwindcss/oxide-linux-x64-gnu`, `@tailwindcss/oxide-wasm32-wasi`,
   `@tauri-apps/cli-linux-x64-gnu`, `lightningcss-linux-x64-gnu`.
   `license-checker` last shipped 2022-06-19 (`pnpm view …
time.modified`) and walks the tree with npm's deprecated
   `read-installed` (`lib/index.js:11`, `:298`; `package.json:64`),
   which under pnpm's layout returns nothing transitive; its own
   install warns of seven deprecated subdependencies. A gate built on
   it would pass a GPL package one level down. The fork walks with
   arborist and misses the native binaries — the packages most likely
   to carry a license of their own — and fetches some 130 packages for
   work pnpm already does. Chosen: pnpm's own inventory, which is what
   `--frozen-lockfile` put on disk, judged by a script with no
   dependencies (`.github/scripts/licenses/check.mjs`). Rule 9: no
   devDependency is added — package.json and pnpm-lock.yaml are
   untouched — and `pnpm dlx`, the other option on the card, would have
   resolved the checker's own dependency tree from the registry on
   every run, unpinned: the wrong shape for a supply-chain gate. Spec
   §5.3 says so now.

4. _Allow-list and scope._ The list is
   `.github/scripts/licenses/allow-list.txt`: deny.toml's eleven
   licenses in the same order, plus two the current tree needs and the
   Rust tree has never had — `BlueOak-1.0.0` (the glob 14 line) and
   `Python-2.0` (argparse). Both are permissive and OSI-approved in the
   SPDX License List 3.29.0 (2026-09-16); `Python-2.0` is FSF-libre as
   well. The check covers the whole tree, devDependencies included —
   the scope of `pnpm audit` here and of cargo-deny over Cargo.lock —
   because a devDependency imported from app code still ships, and the
   gate should not depend on the classification being right. Reading
   an expression: `OR` needs one listed alternative, `AND` every
   operand, `X WITH Y` listed verbatim — cargo-deny's reading of
   deny.toml; `Unknown`, `UNLICENSED`, non-SPDX strings and anything
   unparsable fail closed. `check.test.mjs` pins the parity with
   deny.toml as an oracle (every deny.toml license present; the
   additions exactly the two above), so the two lists cannot drift
   apart silently.

5. _cargo audit's policy._ Defaults, no ignores: a vulnerability
   advisory exits 1; unmaintained, unsound and yanked stay warnings,
   which is deny.toml's own tolerance for transitive unmaintained
   crates (`unmaintained = "workspace"`). `-D warnings` on the current
   Cargo.lock exits 1 with "7 denied warnings found" — the gate would
   be red on day one, so it is not used. deny.toml is untouched.

Solution — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

- `lint`, after `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and ahead of the fmt
  and clippy steps (cheapest first): `pnpm audit` — the full tree;
  exits 1 on any advisory at or above low (the documented default
  level, pnpm.io/cli/audit) and on a registry it cannot reach.
  `--ignore-registry-errors` would turn the latter into a pass and is
  deliberately absent. Then `node --test
.github/scripts/licenses/check.test.mjs`, then `pnpm licenses list
--json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/licenses.json" && node
.github/scripts/licenses/check.mjs …` — a file, not a pipe, so each
  exit status is the step's own (rule 5); an empty or unreadable
  inventory is exit 2, never "no packages, no problems".
- `deny`: `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` (only so that `cargo` can
  dispatch to the subcommand; nothing compiles);
  `taiki-e/install-action@v2` with `tool: cargo-audit` and
  `fallback: none`. The action installs the release binary — the
  static musl build on Linux x64 — and checks the archive against the
  SHA-256 pinned in its manifest (`manifests/cargo-audit.json`: 0.23.0
  as "latest" at v2.90.8; the x86_64-musl hash `4f01c74e…` is also
  GitHub's digest for that asset, reproduced on the downloaded
  archive). `fallback: none` removes the cargo-binstall branch, the
  one the README says is handed `github.token`. Then `cargo audit`
  (placed first, so a published vulnerability shows before the docker
  build of cargo-deny), then the `EmbarkStudios/cargo-deny-action@v2`
  step unchanged.
- No cache for any of the three gates: the advisory database and the
  registry answer are fetched on every run, so none can go stale by
  construction; a failed fetch fails its step.

Failure paths, each exercised rather than reasoned (cargo-audit 0.23.0 —
the gnu and the musl release binary alike — with `--db` pointed at a
scratch directory):

- `pnpm audit`: exit 0 on the current lockfile; exit 1 on the pre-T-323
  lockfile (`git show 21ed8f8^:…` — four advisories, 2 high, 2
  moderate); exit 1 with `ERR_PNPM_AUDIT_BAD_RESPONSE` against
  `--registry http://127.0.0.1:9`, and exit 0 for the same run with
  `--ignore-registry-errors`.
- `cargo audit`: exit 0 on the current Cargo.lock ("7 allowed warnings
  found"); exit 1 on a scratch lockfile with `smallvec 0.6.9`
  (RUSTSEC-2021-0003, RUSTSEC-2019-0012, RUSTSEC-2019-0009) and on one
  with `rustls 0.23.30` (four advisories; its yanked flag reported as
  an allowed warning); exit 1 when the advisory database cannot be
  fetched.
- License check: exit 0 on the real inventory ("257 installed packages
  under 9 license identifiers"); exit 1 on the same tree after
  `pnpm add` of three local fixture packages — `GPL-3.0-only`, no
  license field (`Unknown`), `(MIT OR Apache-2.0) AND CDDL-1.0` —
  naming each. Before an install, `pnpm licenses list --json` puts
  every package under `Unknown`, which the checker refuses as well.
- The checker's own suite: 8 tests, and 28 mutations of `check.mjs`
  and the allow-list (the verdict forced true, trailing tokens
  ignored, OR and AND swapped, the `WITH` exception dropped, the
  empty-inventory and shape guards removed, the length cap removed or
  off by one, stdin unread, each exit code zeroed, a deny.toml license
  removed from the list, a third addition) — every one turns the suite
  red. The two expectations the first run exposed as wrong were the
  tests' (a `LicenseRef-…` id is a well-formed entry; `AND` binds
  tighter than `OR`), not the checker's.

Honest boundaries. (a) The JS license gate covers what is installed on
the Linux x64 runner: pnpm's list is of installed packages, so the
Windows and macOS binaries are not in it — the host-target scope
cargo-deny has by default (deny.toml sets no `[graph] targets`). (b)
`pnpm audit` is as strict as its configuration: `audit.ignore` and
`audit.level` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` would weaken it, and neither is
there today. (c) `taiki-e/install-action@v2` floats — the action's
major tag and, with it, cargo-audit's version (the manifest's "latest"),
under the README's dependency cooldown of one to a few days; pinning
`@v2.90.8` would pin both and is the owner's call (the `deny` step
floats the same way). (d)
A CI-side change: nothing ran on GitHub from the worktree. Proved
locally: the tools' behavior on the real lockfiles with the release
binaries, actionlint 1.7.12 with shellcheck clean on both workflow
files, YAML parse sanity. The push-time run is the proof for the action
mechanics.

Checks, exit codes: `pnpm audit` 0; the license check 0; `node --test
.github/scripts/licenses/check.test.mjs` 0; `pnpm run lint` 0 (the new
`.mjs` files are in its scope); `pnpm run format:check` 0; `cargo deny
check` not run — deny.toml is untouched. No Rust suite was run
(CI-side change).

Follow-ups for the board, outside this card: ARCHITECTURE.md's CI
bullets for `lint` and `deny` do not list the new steps (true, but
incomplete — one docs touch); CONTRIBUTING.md's local check list could
gain `cargo audit`, `pnpm audit` and the license two-liner; the gates
run on push and pull_request only, so a vulnerability published after
a merge is seen at the next push — a scheduled run of the three gates
in a small separate workflow would close that window; the allow-list's
two npm-only additions are a policy the owner may want to confirm;
`build (ubuntu-24.04)` is absent from the required checks (seen in the
protection listing; older than this card).

Reviews, two rounds on two models, both read-only (the worktree's HEAD,
status and diff hash identical before and after each):

- Round 1, deepseek-v4.1-flash (report
  `.opencode/reviews/t228-round1.md`): APPROVE, 0×P0/P1/P2, 1×P3 —
  taken in the amend. The checker's usage header said CI runs "exactly
  these two lines" while CI writes the inventory to `$RUNNER_TEMP` and
  chains the commands with `&&`; the header now says "the same two
  commands" and writes the inventory outside the repo. The reviewer
  re-derived the cargo-audit exit semantics from the RustSec source
  (`cargo-audit/src/presenter.rs`, `should_exit_with_failure`), read
  install-action's `action.yml` to confirm that `fallback: none`
  removes the `github.token` branch, and re-measured the dead-registry
  and pre-T-323 cases.
- Round 2, hy4-flash-free (report `.opencode/reviews/t228-round2.md`):
  APPROVE, no finding at any level. It re-ran six mutations of its own
  on a copy of the checker (each turned the suite red) and the fixture
  inventories through the real CLI (exit 1 / 1 / 1 for the three
  offending licenses, 2 for empty, non-JSON and wrong-shaped input).

### D-185 — T-325: the phase-2 abort stamps `finished_at` with the abort's OWN instant through the `run_with_abort_clock` seam (production: the real clock); D-132's round-1 P3-1 declined the same point and is reversed; MAIN-027 and every other `finished_at` consumer grep-verified unaffected — 2026-11-23

Problem: the 2026-11-23 project review (its P3-2, verified by the
owner) found the phase-2 abort path handing the run's BACKUP instant
to `abort_run` as `finished_at`: `created_at = db002_stamp(now)` is
phase 2's entry instant — the `jiff::Timestamp::now()` the `sync_run`
command passes at its call (`commands.rs:1204-1210`) — and the abort
transaction wrote that where the abort's own moment belongs. The whole
copy pass (three streaming passes per file over possibly dead
volumes) and the abort sweep vanished from the run's duration: a slow
backup that aborted read as a run that ended when its backups began.
Re-verified present at this task's base (`ae83a87`; main had moved
past the review's revision): the red run in the Tests section
reproduces it on the untouched tree. Three facts make it a defect,
not a reading:

- _The column's documented meaning._ The store's own rule for the
  terminal stamp — `finished_at` "IS stamped — the moment the row
  reached its terminal status, exactly what the column names for
  `aborted` rows too" (`crates/eunomia-store/src/sync_runs.rs`,
  `mark_interrupted_runs`' docs) — and the wire DTO's doc on
  `SyncRunSummary::finished_at` ("When the run reached its terminal
  status (DB-002)", `commands.rs:710-711`) both name the abort's
  moment, never an earlier one.
- _The sibling aborts read the clock at the abort._ Phase 1's
  `E_DISK_FULL` tail (`values::now_utc()` right before its
  transaction, `sync_phase1.rs:439`) and the command's `stop_run` /
  `stop_run_if_running` (`commands.rs:1383`, `:1406`).
- _History._ D-132's round-1 review raised exactly this as its P3-1
  and T-115 declined it: "§6.2 pins no abort-stamp accuracy, a second
  clock parameter breaks the determinism the fixed instant buys, and
  in production both stamps come from the same real clock within one
  run". The last clause is the error — the two stamps are a whole
  copy pass apart, and that gap is the duration a report loses. This
  entry reverses the decline; a dated addendum beside D-132's P3-1
  points here. (§9.4 and §6.2 do stay silent on abort-stamp accuracy
  — the ruling rests on the column's own documented meaning, not on a
  spec sentence, which is why the fix is a card and not a spec PR.)

Solution: `src-tauri/src/sync_phase2.rs` gains ONE clock seam; no
other behavior moves.

- _The seam: `run_with_abort_clock`._ `run` keeps its five
  parameters — they are the `sync_run` command's wiring
  (`commands.rs:1204-1210`) and `commands.rs` is a frozen zone for
  this task (T-077's) — and becomes the production entry: it
  delegates with `Timestamp::now`.
  `run_with_abort_clock(…, abort_clock: impl FnOnce() -> Timestamp)`
  is the body. `FnOnce`, because one run aborts at most once and the
  clock is consulted on the abort path only; no `Send`/`'static`,
  because it is read on the async side, before the transaction
  closure is built. The command layer's own `sync_run` /
  `sync_run_with` shape, and phase 3's injected `clock` precedent
  (D-133).
- _Where the clock is read: once, right before the verdict
  transaction, after the sweep._ That is the moment the row goes
  terminal — the phase-1 abort's and `stop_run`'s posture — and not
  the copy failure: the abort sweep is the run's time too (a deletion
  riding §9.5's ladder takes up to 1.3 s per copy), and the run, with
  its `sync_running` flag, lives until the abort has committed. The
  answer is stamped through the module's own `db002_stamp` — the
  `values::now_utc` spelling its unit test pins — so production's
  stamp has exactly the shape of every other terminal stamp. The read
  point is pinned, not only documented: the seam test's clock answers
  one instant while a swept copy is still on disk and a later one once
  it is gone, so a read before the sweep stamps the wrong literal
  (mutant M4 below).
- _What did NOT change._ `now` (the run's backup instant, D-061)
  still resolves into every copy name and every record's
  `created_at`; the abort stamp is a SECOND instant of the run, so
  record and name still cannot disagree. `commands.rs` is untouched:
  the command passes `jiff::Timestamp::now()` exactly as before. The
  store's `abort_run` is untouched in behavior — it always wrote the
  caller's timestamp verbatim; the defect was the caller's argument.
  Its doc now states the contract the defect slipped through: the
  moment is THIS abort's, and "the store writes the caller's text
  verbatim and cannot tell the two apart". No new crate, no unsafe,
  no deny ignore; nothing user-provided reaches any diagnostic.
- _Consumers of an aborted run's `finished_at` — grep-verified
  unaffected._ MAIN-027 (`last_success_finished_at`, the only
  statement in the tree that filters or orders by the column) filters
  `status = 'success'`: an `aborted` row never matches, so the overall
  last-success time cannot move (§9.4 phase 4 step 4). The P3-4
  wrapper cannot overwrite the stamp: `stop_run_if_running` decides
  by the ROW (`running` only, `commands.rs:1409-1414`), and phase 2's
  in-phase abort left it `aborted` — the no-op `ipc_tests.rs` already
  pins over `finished_at` ("the terminal row is never rewritten").
  `finish_run` and the startup `interrupted` sweep are each scoped to
  `running` rows; the `sync_runs` retention (`action_log::cleanup`)
  orders by `started_at DESC, id DESC`, not `finished_at`. No code
  computes a run duration today — no `finished_at`/`started_at`
  difference in `src-tauri`, the crates or `src/` — so the card's
  "reports" are the row itself plus the readers not yet landed
  (`sync_last_result`, the history UI), which now read a truthful
  stamp; the wire type (`string | null`) is unchanged, and the phase-2
  abort answers `Err`, so no summary carries the stamp today.
- _`sync_pipeline_tests.rs` (T-126) pinned nothing to update._ The
  suite has no abort-path test at all — zero occurrences of `abort`,
  `E_BACKUP_FAILED` or `BackupFailed`; its thirteen tests cover
  creation, overwrite, the markers, external edits, library
  operations, the watch, unchanged runs and the sync times — so no
  expectation there encoded the old behavior, and the file is not
  touched. A pipeline-level abort test with a measurable pause would
  need a clock seam on the COMMAND (`commands.rs`, frozen here): a
  board follow-up, below.

Tests (Bug-Driven Development; `src-tauri/src/sync_phase2_tests.rs` —
two new tests, one expectation corrected, the suite's header and
`fixed_now`'s doc corrected with it):

- RED FIRST, on the untouched tree:
  `the_production_entry_stamps_the_abort_with_the_real_clock`. The
  production entry `run` is driven with a backup instant fixed at
  `2000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` (far in the past, so the ordering cannot
  depend on the day the suite runs); the row must carry an instant
  between the test's own two clock readings, compared at the DB-002
  millisecond (the stamp truncates) — no sleep anywhere. At base it
  failed with `finished_at = 2000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`: the injected
  backup instant, written as the abort's end.
- The card's criterion, over the seam:
  `an_abort_after_a_measurable_pause_stamps_finished_at_after_created_at`.
  The clock models a slow backup and has one answer per moment of the
  abort, keyed on what the phase itself has done by then: the backup
  instant (`2026-11-21T10:30:00.123Z`) until the failing copy has
  answered (the injector's own `before_fail` hook flips a flag); the
  failure's instant (`2026-11-21T10:30:47.000Z`) while the swept copy
  is still on disk; the abort instant (`2026-11-21T10:30:47.500Z`,
  47.377 s after the backup instant) once the sweep has deleted it.
  Asserted: `finished_at > created_at`, compared as instants;
  `finished_at` equals the abort instant's DB-002 literal — an
  independent oracle, never an output of `db002_stamp`; and the swept
  copy's `discarded` record still carries `created_at = CREATED_AT`
  under the copy name the backup instant stamps (D-061 intact — and
  the record is the proof the copy existed for the middle state).
  No production seam and no sleep: the clock reads a flag and the
  disk, both joined before the read point. The three states separate
  "read at the phase's entry", "read at the failure" and "read after
  the sweep" — mutants M2 and M4 below.
- Corrected expectation — a test that had encoded the defect, not a
  check evaded:
  `a_copy_error_aborts_the_run_sweeps_the_copies_and_resets_the_rows`
  asserted `finished_at == CREATED_AT` ("the fixed stamp") and its
  docs said one value pins "the record `created_at` … and the aborted
  run's `finished_at`" — the same reading D-132 recorded. It now
  drives the seam with the constant abort clock and asserts
  `ABORTED_AT`. It was the only assertion in the tree of a phase-2
  abort's stamp value (every `_tests.rs` and the store suite
  grepped), so leaving it would have kept the bug pinned; the three
  stamp-asserting tests are the suite's whole change of expectations.
- Mutation record — four mutants, each applied to the final tree, run
  with `--no-fail-fast`, then restored byte-for-byte (sha256 checked
  before and after every run):
  M1, the original defect (`abort_run(…, &entry_stamp, …)`) → exactly
  the three stamp-asserting tests red, 14/17 green;
  M2, the clock read at the phase's ENTRY, before the copy pass →
  only the stateful-clock test red (`finished_at = CREATED_AT`),
  16/17 — the real-clock and the constant-clock tests cannot see it;
  M3, the production entry wiring its own `now` as the abort clock →
  only the production-entry test red, 16/17 — the seam tests cannot
  see a wrong production wiring;
  M4, the clock read right after the copy pass, BEFORE the sweep →
  only the stateful-clock test red (`finished_at` = the failure's
  literal, `…47.000Z`), 16/17 — the documented read point's own
  oracle (the round-1 review's P3-3).
  Every new or corrected assertion therefore has a mutant that turns
  it red, and each test has one only it can catch.
- Store: no test changed. `abort_run_finishes_the_run_without_touching_counters_or_rows`
  (`crates/eunomia-store/tests/sync_runs.rs`) already pins the
  caller's stamp verbatim, with a `FINISHED_AT` distinct from
  `STARTED_AT` — the store's half was never wrong, and no store-level
  oracle can tell the caller's right instant from its wrong one.

Checks: `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2 cargo fmt --all -- --check`,

### D-186 — T-322: the database session tail is one shared function (`start_database_session`) run by the `setup` hook and by the recovery commands, the two service buses parked in a managed `StateServices` slot until a database is published, and the start spent exactly once per session — 2026-11-23

Problem: P1-1 of the 2026-11-23 project review
(`.opencode/reviews/project-review-2026-11-23.md`, confirmed by its
`-verification.md`): after a successful `db_restore_backup`/
`db_recreate`, `run_recovery` reopened, swept, copied and published
the database — and nothing else. The handle was not even `mut`, so no
commit hook; no dirty service, no watcher, no availability listener,
no availability startup pass, no retention task. Until a restart
`state://dirty` and `state://file-changed` never emitted on their own,
external edits went undetected and the daily retention did not run —
the UI silently under-reported unsaved and external changes right
after the user recovered data. D-121 had recorded the gap and promised
that "the recovery commands' task re-arms both"; T-024 landed the
commands without it, and T-258 (D-147's P3-5) mirrored only the sweep.

Re-verification at the base (the card's line numbers were revision
fd00673's; everything was located by content at `f8b545a`):

- _By reading._ `run_recovery` (`commands.rs`) ended
  `app.manage(database); Ok(())` after the sweep and the daily copy;
  `database` was an immutable binding. By grep, the production call
  sites of `set_commit_hook`, the two `spawn_service`s,
  `listen_availability`, `spawn_daily_cleanup` and `spawn_recheck`
  existed only in `lib.rs`'s `setup` hook.
- _At runtime._ the four recovery batteries below, written first, were
  red against the base code: the restore battery timed out on "the
  startup availability recheck must report the gone folder", the other
  three on "the dirty service ran only 0 passes, waiting for 1".

Four questions were open before a line was written.

- _Where do the two bus receiving halves live between the hook's
  recovery-mode return and the recovery?_ Before: locals of the
  `setup` closure, dropped by its early `return Ok(())`. They cannot
  be rebuilt at recovery time — the halves belong to the buses the
  managed `DirtyState`/`FileWatchState` own, and tauri keeps the FIRST
  managed value of a type: verified in the installed 2.12.6,
  `src/state.rs:118-127` (`StateManager::set` answers `!already_set`
  and inserts nothing on a duplicate), `:142-146` (`get` panics with
  "state not found for type" on a missing one) and `src/lib.rs`'s
  `Manager::unmanage` — `unsafe`, deprecated since 2.3.0, its own doc
  naming `Mutex<Option<_>>` + `Option::take` as the supported shape.
  Decision: one managed slot, `StateServices`
  (`Mutex<Option<(Receiver<Trigger>, Receiver<Command>)>>`, `lib.rs`),
  managed beside the states that own the buses — before anything that
  can fail — and taken by the shared tail. The same fact corrects
  `RECOVERY_OPERATION`'s doc in `commands.rs`, which claimed `manage`
  "panics on a duplicate state": it does not; it answers `false` and
  keeps the first, which is what makes an ungated double recovery a
  silent discard of the loser's reopen rather than a crash.
- _How much of the tail is shared?_ All of it — the §9.4 sweep, the
  DB-022 commit hook, the ERR-001 daily copy, the publication and the
  four services:
  `start_database_session(app: &AppHandle<R>, database: Db)`
  (`lib.rs`). The recovery path had mirrored three of the five steps (T-258 added the sweep to the mirror — the second copy
  D-161's rule is about); one function ends the mirroring. Order and
  spellings are unchanged, so every `lib.rs` text pin stayed green
  untouched: `db_tests.rs`'s open → daily copy → manage → retention
  spawn (no `?`/`return` between copy and manage), `ipc_tests.rs`'s
  open → sweep → hook → manage, and the raw "exactly once" counts of
  the dirty and watch wiring. Those scans read `lib.rs` alone: they
  see the tail's body, not its callers — the hook's call of the tail
  and the recovery's lack of a mirror were unpinned until round 1
  found it (below, M12 and the pin that kills it).
- _Which thread runs the tail in recovery?_ Before, the sweep and the
  daily copy ran on the async worker after the `spawn_blocking` join —
  a `VACUUM INTO`, i.e. a file copy, on a worker (SYS-001; the module
  doc's own claim was false for those two steps). Now the tail runs
  inside the same blocking closure, after the reopen and the audit
  lines, whose order is unchanged. The hook runs it on the main thread
  before the event loop, as before.
- _What does a second start do?_ Three layers, each with its own
  evidence. (a) The command: a recovery in a session that already runs
  a database is refused before any file moves (the existing
  `db_recreate_is_rejected_once_the_database_is_running`) — and since
  round 1 it is refused UNDER the operation gate, which is now taken
  first. The guard used to run before the gate: a check-then-lock
  window in which a restore that passed the check, waited, and took
  the gate after a concurrent recovery had finished would preserve
  that recovery's working database away, publish nothing and answer
  success (pre-existing; round 1's P2-1, re-verified by reading
  `StateManager::set` before it was taken). (b) The
  tail: a call that finds a database already managed stops at
  `manage`'s `false` — the handle it was handed is dropped unpublished
  and nothing is armed. (c) The take: the parked halves are taken only
  AFTER a successful publication, so a start is spent only by the call
  that publishes a database and arms over it; every reachable failure
  of a recovery precedes the tail, which leaves the start unspent for
  the user's next attempt. A fourth branch — "published, but nothing
  parked" — was written first and found unreachable by mutation
  (M8 below survived: layer (b)'s return shields it); it is now a
  reasoned `expect`, the house shape for a broken composition (the
  module docs of `dirty_recalc.rs`), and removing layer (b) is killed
  by it (M11).

One ordering that was implicit in the hook is now stated at its step:
the retention handle is cloned AFTER the hook is installed — the hook
is a per-clone field of `Db` (`Db::set_commit_hook`; the test suites'
`hooked_handle` documents it), so a clone taken earlier would run the
retention task's prunes without the commit seam.

Solution: `src-tauri/src/lib.rs` — `StateServices` and
`start_database_session`; the hook parks the halves
(`app.manage(StateServices::parked(..))`, :473) and its post-open tail
is one call (:597); `commands.rs` — `run_recovery` runs the tail inside
its blocking closure (:312); `db.rs` — the hook, daily-copy and sweep
docs name their one caller (the tail, both open paths).

Testing (BDD, red first). Five behavior batteries and — since round
1 — two wiring pins in `ipc_tests.rs`; the harness
`recovery_mode_app()` grew into the hook's real recovery-mode state —
the three service states, the parked slot, and the three state events
mounted (`tauri_specta` 2.0.0-rc.29 `src/event.rs:45-53`: without
`mount_events` an emit or listen panics on the registry lookup, which
is why the old harness, `DataRoot` only, could not have hosted them):

- `db_restore_arms_the_state_services_over_the_restored_world` — the
  card's definition of done plus the other two services' startup
  runs. The copy carries a whole world: a synced project, a project
  whose folder is gone, and a journal over its limit (`log.max_entries`
  at the §6.5 floor, 1000, with 1050 rows). After the restore over
  mock IPC: the availability startup pass reports the gone folder;
  the retention task's startup run brings the journal to 1000; both
  wires are silent over the clean world; then an external edit of the
  target file emits `state://file-changed` (`external_changed`), and a
  library commit through the store repository — the write path a
  library command takes — emits `state://dirty` (`dirty: true`).
- `db_recreate_arms_the_state_services_over_the_fresh_database` — the
  recreate half: one transaction (the project and its first
  assignment) drives the recalculation onto the wire; after the
  after-sync seam brings the watch set up to date, an external edit
  reaches it.
- `a_second_recovery_in_one_session_arms_no_second_set_of_services` —
  the retry is rejected (`E_VALIDATION`, "a database is already
  running") and arms nothing: the pass counters hold across a settle
  window (every spawned service starts with its own trigger, which
  runs a pass at once), and one availability diff is exactly ONE full
  watch pass — the listener registered once, and still registered.
- `a_failed_recovery_arms_nothing_and_a_later_recovery_still_arms` — a
  restore of a missing copy is rejected before anything is touched;
  nothing is published or started; the recreate after it arms.
- `the_shared_tail_publishes_a_database_and_arms_the_services_once_per_session`
  — the tail driven the way the hook drives it (the hook itself cannot
  run on the mock runtime), then a second call over another database:
  the first database stays the session's (a probe marker read through
  a handle fetched AFTER the second call), no counter moves, and a
  commit still reaches the wire.
- `the_setup_hook_runs_the_shared_tail_and_the_recovery_path_mirrors_none_of_it`
  and `the_recovery_gate_is_taken_before_the_recovery_mode_guard` —
  the two wiring pins round 1 showed were missing: the hook calls the
  tail exactly once, after the open, with nothing after it; the
  recovery path calls it exactly once and mirrors none of the tail's
  steps; the operation gate precedes the recovery-mode guard.

Mutations (each restored after its run; M8 is the one that survived):

- M1, the hook not installed → 4 of 5 red (the one-shot battery does
  not depend on it).
- M2, the dirty service not spawned → 5 of 5 red.
- M3, the watcher not spawned → 5 of 5 red.

- M11, layer (b)'s guard removed → the shared-tail battery red through

- M12 (round 1), the hook's call of the tail replaced by a drop → the

- M13 (round 1), the guard moved back before the gate → the new order

- M14 (round 1), the tail made to publish the second database → the

Honest boundaries:

- The watcher's own startup degrade (D-155) now applies to the
  recovery path identically — a refused watcher backend leaves no
  watching until restart. Not reachable through the real backend at
  the app layer (D-148), so it is unpinned here too.
- The new batteries follow the hardened cross-platform shapes — D-181's
  draining convergence before the file act, deadline-based event

- A second call of the tail is unreachable through the production

- The hook's call of the tail is pinned by a text scan — added after

  (`docs/manual-smoke.md`, pending the recovery screen).
- "A failed recovery leaves the start unspent" is proven for the
  failure before any file moves (the missing copy). The documented

  the reopen — fails inside `Db::open`, before the tail, by the same

- Four modules outside this card's zone still attribute the startup
  wiring to the `setup` hook alone (verified by reading each line):
  `dirty_recalc.rs` :10-13, :118-122 and :470 ("the `setup` hook's
  one call"), `file_watch.rs` :36, :139-144 and :1100-1102,
  `availability.rs` :11-13, `retention.rs` :17-20 and :97-99. Their

- Unchanged and not this card's: a library edit flips the

- P3-2 (taken): the retention-clone-after-hook comment was framed as
  load-bearing; the prunes touch the journal and the runs, not the
  build's inputs, so nothing observable rides on it — the comment says
  so now and keeps the shape.
- P3-3 (taken): the restore battery awaited the retention prune before
  the dirty startup pass, so "the startup pass ran" could be read as
  the prune's own pass; the startup passes are awaited first (the
  service's startup permit is queued before the retention task exists)
  and the silence is asserted after both.
- P3-4 (noted, no action): the event deadline is 5 s and the journal
  poll 20 s; the asymmetry is deliberate — a missing wire event fails
  fast, the prune may legitimately take longer on a loaded runner.

### D-187 — T-083: the `library_get` command — labels are active-project chips, the tree is one flat position-ordered vector, variants ride inline with the emptiness flag — 2026-11-23

Problem: the §7.10 Library module's read command (`library_get`, spec
§7.3 LIB-001/008/014, spec-table D-14, LIB-032, §7.10) had three
readings the card leaves open, each recorded here before the code
(rule 1):

- _Which projects do LIB-001's "colored labels of the projects where
  at least one variant is assigned" cover?_ **Active projects only.**
  The library list is the row header of the §7.4 matrix, whose columns
  are the ACTIVE projects in `sort_order` (MAIN-001); an archived
  project keeps its assignment rows (DB-014) but is no column, so a
  label for it would name a cell the screen does not render. The
  card's acceptance criterion — labels match assignments — is read as:
  the labels on an instruction row are exactly the ACTIVE projects
  with a `project_instructions` row on that instruction, each label
  naming the assigned variant.
- _What exactly is "variants with an emptiness flag" (LIB-014)?_ The
  instruction entry carries its ACTIVE variants inline — id, name,
  `is_main` (DB-010; the click-assign default and the LIB-024 disable
  both read it), `is_empty` (content empty after the store's fold; the
  LIB-014 icon). The card's "number of variants" is `variant_count`,
  the length of that same list, so the two facts cannot drift. Variant
  CONTENT is deliberately not served: the card's field list is the
  tree's, and no §7.10 command carries the editor's text yet — the
  carrier for MAIN-006's tooltip text and the editor body is the
  variant-editor command family's concern (follow-up in the task
  report).
- _Item order and identity on the wire._ One flat vector in `position`
  order, the order expressed as collection order and the position
  NUMBER not repeated (the core `library` precedent — one fact, one
  place). A tagged enum serves the two kinds; `include_hidden`
  (`Option<bool>`, default active-only, `true` widens — the
  `projects_list` precedent) backs D-14's "Show hidden" toggle, and
  hidden instructions keep their labels (DB-013: assignments are
  kept).

The LIB-032 skip flag reuses `eunomia_core::gaps::heading_level_gaps`
(D-073) — the command builds core `LibraryItem`s from the served
rows (instructions with an empty variant vector: the walk reads
headings only) and marks the heading at each report's `to_index`
`level_skipped`. Hidden instructions are transparent to the pair walk
(the gaps module's own rule), so the flag set is identical under
either `include_hidden` value; the indices are taken over the SERVED
collection, which is the list the UI renders.

Everything runs in one `Db::run` transaction (D-037): the items read,
the active-variants read, the active-projects read and the
active-projects' assignments read — one snapshot, no per-row queries;
the label join, the variant grouping and the gap walk are linear Rust
passes over data already in memory (rule 6). A read: no SYS-005 gate,
no journal (D-051), no file I/O — nothing to probe, so no extra
`spawn_blocking` pass beyond the executor's own. `LibraryError`
normalizes through `library_store_to_app_error` (the D-093 boundary's
planned seam: `Sql` → the shared SQLite classifier, `Member` → the
D-037 fallback with a class-only diagnostic naming the column —
never the stored value, rule 8; write-path variants arrive only if a
future command reuses the mapper and map to the family fallback).

### D-188 — T-328: the `instruction_create` / `instruction_update` / `instruction_hide` / `instruction_restore` commands — the create dialog's "section" read as the end-of-section placement, the rename/hide/restore verified no-ops, and no SYS-005 gate for library edits — 2026-11-24

Problem: the batch of the three absorbed cards (T-084 create,
T-085 rename, T-086 hide/restore) lands the first four §7.10 Library
commands over the already-landed repositories (T-081 `library`,
T-082 `library_versions`) and validators (T-063). Five points were
open: (1) what the T-084 card's "text at the specified position
(section)" takes on the wire — the §7.3 LIB-002 create dialog and
scenario S3 both say "pick a section", but no §7.10 signature spells
the parameter; (2) whether the T-085 DoD's "renaming to the same
name creates no version" is the version layer's ALG-070 hash gate
alone or a command-level no-op; (3) whether hide/restore record and
journal on an idempotent re-run (the store's `hide_item`/
`restore_item` are idempotent by D-093's design and hand the caller
no "changed" signal); (4) whether the commands run the SYS-005
`E_SYNC_RUNNING` gate the project-changing commands run; (5) which
§10 code rejects the DB-016 marker line.

Readings chosen (Rule 1, recorded before implementation):

- **(1) The section rule.** `instruction_create(name, text,
section)` takes `section: Option<String>` — a heading row id.
  `Some(id)`: the new instruction is placed at the END of that
  heading's ALG-060 range (the item before the next heading of level
  ≤ the heading's level, or the table end) — the same "end of the
  section" target LIB-032 gives an instruction dropped on a heading,
  so drag-drop and create-place agree. `None` (root, the dialog's
  "no section"): the end of the prefix before the FIRST heading —
  the only place an instruction has no heading above it (ALG-021);
  with no headings in the table the whole table is the root, so
  `None` is the table end. A `section` that names no row or names an
  instruction is the `E_VALIDATION` field refusal of the `section`
  field (headings are the only section identity, MAIN-015). The
  placement composes the store's own two functions — `create_item`
  (appends at `MAX(position)+1`) then `move_item` to the computed
  target — inside the command's one transaction, so no new store
  seam and no renumbering duplication (the D-179 "by construction,
  not by copy" posture). The rejected alternative was a raw
  `position: i64` parameter: it moves the ALG-060 range arithmetic
  into every caller (the UI would have to compute section ends), and
  an integer the webview sends is unvalidated structure — the
  id-addressed form keeps the section semantics server-side.
- **(2) Rename-to-same-name is a verified no-op.** The command
  compares the VALIDATED name with the stored title before any
  write; equal answers `Ok(())` with nothing written — no store
  write (the store would restamp `updated_at` for a field-present
  update), no `record_instruction` call, no journal entry (the
  D-115/D-137 verified-no-op precedent). The ALG-070 hash gate would
  absorb the version row anyway; the pre-check keeps the save
  honest end to end: "saving without changes adds none" (LIB-026's
  acceptance) covers the journal and the row too, not only the
  `revisions` table. The comparison is on the validated (trimmed)
  form against the stored form — the D-075 contract makes those the
  same shape.
- **(3) Hide/restore converge on re-runs.** A hide of an
  already-hidden instruction and a restore of an active one are
  verified no-ops in the same D-115 shape: the row read first, the
  state compared, nothing written, recorded or journaled when the
  requested state is already current. The store's own idempotence
  stays the floor; the command does not re-journal a transition
  that did not happen (a double-clicked eye button converges to one
  journal entry and one `hide` version).
- **(4) No SYS-005 gate.** §5.4 SYS-005's own sentence: "Library
  edits during a sync are allowed; they do not go into the current
  run and stay 'dirty'." The gate is for commands that change
  PROJECTS (`project_update`, `project_remove`, `project_relink`,
  P1 `backup_restore`); these four commands write library rows, and
  the DB-022 commit hook recalculates the dirty set after every
  committed transaction — the honest integration for a library edit
  mid-sync is the dirty flag, not a refusal.
- **(5) `E_CONTENT_RESERVED` for the DB-016 marker line.** DB-016
  says "Saving is rejected with the `E_CONTENT_RESERVED` error", so
  `validate_variant_text`'s `ReservedContent` arm maps to
  `ErrorCode::ContentReserved` with the marker literal and the
  built-form line number as params; every other validator arm
  (empty/long/line-break/NUL name, too-long/NUL text) maps to
  `E_VALIDATION` with the field/value/reason envelope.

The journal shape (LOG-001, D-051): `instruction_create` writes ONE
`instruction.created` entry — the main variant is part of the
instruction's birth (LIB-002: the create dialog always produces the
pair), not a separate user action — while the VERSION layer records
both entities (one `create` version for the instruction, one for
the variant, ALG-071's own per-entity `rev_no`); `instruction_update`
writes `instruction.changed`, hide and restore their own members.
Every command runs inside ONE `Db::run` transaction (§6.9 "an entity
is never saved partly"; D-037/D-051), versions recorded with
`history.max_revisions` read in the same transaction (ALG-072's
caller contract), the journal entry inside the operation's own
transaction.

Verification. BDD red first: the whole battery was written before
the implementation and run against deliberate stubs — every behavior
test red (the stubs' refusals satisfied none of the expected
outcomes) — then green on the real implementation. Nineteen
mock-IPC tests in `ipc_tests.rs` (the `library_app` healthy shape,
seeds through the T-081/T-082 repositories, the build asserted
through the §9.1 snapshot + §9.2 builder the sync itself uses — the
independent oracle for T-086's "a hidden instruction is not in the
build"), six unit tests of the pure mapping seams in `commands.rs`'s
own suite, and fifteen mock-layer tests in
`src/ipc/mock/commands.spec.ts` (the wire twins: the same §6.9 order,
the same envelopes, the same D-188 rules; the mock store gained the
`library` rows the fixture generator already built — the known
limits, no version table and no assignment rows, are stated in the
file). Mutations: 39 scripted mutations in all (28 against the Rust
command file — the duplicate envelope, the marker line's own code,
both version recordings, the created variant's main-variant shape,
the journal member of each command, the section placement, its root
half and its `level <= own` half under both wrong readings, the
same-name/hide/restore no-op guards, the by-id kind and existence
guards, the §6.9 name and text validation and their fixed order,
the §6.5 limit read, the actual writes of rename and hide — and 11
against the mock twin — the duplicate check, the marker code, the
placement, the root target, the no-op guard, the hide flip, the
restore refusal, the ASCII-only twin fold, the
section-before-duplicate order, the fixed-point leading edge, the
save-folded storage); every one was KILLED by its oracle
test, and the mutated file was restored byte-for-byte after each
(`cmp` against a backup). Checks, all exit 0: `cargo fmt --check`,
`cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`,
`cargo nextest run --workspace --test-threads=4` (1713 tests),
`pnpm test` (307 tests), `pnpm run format:check`, `pnpm run lint`,
`pnpm run typecheck`; `src/bindings.ts` regenerated through the
export pin test (the first run red as documented, the committed file
regenerated, the pin green since). Docs brought to the landed truth
(Rule 11): ARCHITECTURE.md's registered-commands enumeration,
`docs/manual-smoke.md`'s pending-surfaces paragraph and the S3
entry's Pending line (the create/rename/lifecycle backend is in
place; the assignment step's backend and the UI surfaces are not),
the `commands.rs` and `ipc_tests.rs` module docs, and
`src/ipc/mode.spec.ts`'s pinned command set.

### D-189 — The five variant commands (T-329): the command contract, the version/journal gating, and the layering against D-125's UI rulings — 2026-11-24

Problem: the batch card T-329 (absorbing T-087…T-091) lands the §7.10
Library-module variant commands (`variant_create`, `variant_update`,
`variant_set_main`, `variant_delete`, `variant_restore`) over the
already-landed store repository, §6.9 validators, version recorder and
journal — and the sources left five readings open.

Solution — the chosen readings, in the order the card lists its parts:

1. **Placement: a new module, not `commands.rs`.** The commands live in
   `src-tauri/src/variants.rs` (tests in `variants_tests.rs`), the
   `scan.rs` precedent for a §7.10 command group: the parallel siblings
   T-083/T-328 (same base commit) edit `commands.rs` from their own
   cards, and a separate module is the minimal conflict surface the
   batch brief demands.
2. `variant_create(instruction_id, name, source)` with
   `source ∈ {copy_main, empty}` (LIB-017…022's "a copy of the main
   one or empty"). The name is the CALLER's — the "first free name
   Variant N" prefill is the dialog's affordance (a UI task; the
   command validates §6.9 and the store enforces NOCASE uniqueness);
   `copy_main` reads the main's CURRENT stored content INSIDE the same
   transaction (no TOCTOU with a concurrent edit on the one
   connection, D-037); a created variant is never main (DB-010's
   constructive half — the store's `MainRequired` surfaces a tampered
   no-main instruction, DB-017's surfaced-not-repaired posture).
3. `variant_update(id, name, content)`: both fields optional, `None`
   leaves the field unchanged (the store's `VariantUpdate` shape).
   §10's own rows split the card's "запрет NUL и строк-маркеров
   (E_CONTENT_RESERVED)": NUL and the 262,144-character limit are field
   validation (`E_VALIDATION`, §10's "a field failed validation
   (table 6.9)"); a reserved marker line is `E_CONTENT_RESERVED`
   (§10's literal situation row "the text contains a scheme B marker
   line"). The CRLF→LF fold stays the store's own §6.9 clause (D-076)
   and needs no command-side twin.
4. `variant_delete(id, replacement)`: `None` is LIB-023's
   default-to-main (D-125's C3), `Some` the named successor. Deleting
   the main without a named successor is the typed `E_VALIDATION`
   refusal (the store's `ReplacementRequired` — the card's own words:
   "при удалении основного обязателен новый основной", the successor
   flow D-12's original dialog wording already described: "the user
   picks a new main variant in a dialog"). D-125's C2 ("the main
   variant cannot be deleted at all", §6.4) stays the UI-level rule —
   the disabled Delete button — and the spec's LIB-023/024/025 row
   shows the ANALOGOUS layering for LIB-025 (the last variant: the
   disabled button in the UI, the defensive refusal kept on the
   command and the store behind it); this batch extends that
   layering to the main-variant delete: the command and the store
   keep the store's full contract, the UI simply never sends the
   main-delete without a successor.
5. **Versions and the journal are keyed to the real change.**
   `variant_update` journals `variant.changed` IFF ALG-070 inserted a
   version — the hash gate is §9.8's own definition of "a real change"
   (D-16), so a save without changes writes no version AND no journal
   (the D-051 no-false-claim rule; the store's same-value restamp of
   `updated_at` is its own landed field-write semantics, not fought
   here). create/delete/restore journal unconditionally after a
   genuine transition; `variant_set_main` writes NO version (D-16: the
   main flag is not snapshot-visible) and journals `variant.changed`
   (the action's own "main choice" member). Idempotent re-sends
   (delete on already-deleted, restore on active, set_main on the
   current main) are verified no-ops — nothing written, journaled, or
   versioned (the `projects_reorder` replayed-drag shape).
   `variant.deleted` carries `Details::Bulk { changed }` with the
   moved-assignment count — the number the LIB-023 confirmation names.
6. **SYS-005 does not apply:** §5.4's own sentence — "Library edits
   during a sync are allowed; they do not go into the current run and
   stay dirty" — so the variant commands take no `reject_during_sync`
   gate (unlike the project-changing commands); the DB-022 dirty
   recalculation rides `Db::run`'s commit hook with no extra wiring.
7. **The `LibraryError` mapping (the D-093 normalization this module
   owns):** the typed LIB/DB-010/DB-012 outcomes → `E_VALIDATION` field
   refusals (`id`, `instruction_id`, `variant_name`, `replacement`); a
   corrupt vocabulary cell (`Member`) → the D-037 fallback with a
   class-only `LibraryCorrupt` diagnostic (the T-027 round-2 rule —
   never the stored value); `Sql` → the shared base classifier. Rule-8
   posture: `params` carry fields, reasons, counts and indexes — never
   the variant name or text (`LibraryFieldError`'s members become
   `length`/`index`/`line`/`marker` numbers; no `value` param —
   deliberately stricter than the project-name `rejected_field`
   precedent, because the UI already holds the draft it sent).
8. **The mock layer** wires the generator's held library/assignment
   fixtures into the mock state (its own comment reserved them "for
   the Library/Assignments command tasks") and models the five
   contracts over them — NOCASE uniqueness, the exactly-one-main
   invariant, the delete/restore flow, the `E_*` envelopes.

### D-191 — T-330: one typed heading-update operation, semantic move targets, and atomic library-order persistence — 2026-11-24

Problem: the batch lands `heading_create`, `heading_update`,
`heading_delete` and `items_move` (T-092…T-095). The card explicitly
leaves the T-094 transport open: §7.10 fixes the command name
`heading_update` but not how "Change level" and "Shift branch level ±1"
reach it. The move prose also names UI drop outcomes rather than wire
arguments, while the landed store's `move_item` accepts only one final
1-based position (`crates/eunomia-store/src/library.rs:1211-1281`) and
the core move accepts an insertion gap in the ORIGINAL list, including
the end gap `len` (`crates/eunomia-core/src/reorder.rs:15-54`). Persisting
a whole core permutation through repeated single-row moves would be a
command-layer reimplementation of repository ordering and could become
quadratic in the branch size.

Solution — readings chosen before implementation:

1. **One command, one mutually exclusive operation.**
   `heading_update(id, update)` takes a tagged enum:
   `{"mode":"rename","value":"…"}`,
   `{"mode":"change_level","value":2..=6}`, or
   `{"mode":"shift_branch","value":-1|+1}`. An enum, rather than three
   optional fields, makes "rename and shift" and "two level modes at
   once" unrepresentable; no fifth §7.10 command is invented. The Rust
   core remains the rule owner: `change_heading_level` and
   `shift_branch_level` (`crates/eunomia-core/src/levels.rs:272-483`)
   perform the boundary checks, and their `LevelError` outcomes map to
   `E_VALIDATION` at the IPC boundary. Wire level/delta values are
   `i32`, not `u8`/`i8`: every JSON integer must reach the command's
   validation boundary rather than fail serde before an `AppError`
   exists. The command converts to core's closed types only after the
   heading operand is resolved (round-2 P2). A same-value rename/level
   change is a verified no-op: no row restamp and no journal entry.
2. **Automatic drop alignment extends the same core rule.**
   `shift_branch_to_level(items, index, new_root_level)` joins the
   existing `levels` module and shares its all-or-nothing validation
   pass with the ±1 operation. ALG-062's automatic case needs an
   arbitrary difference within 2–6, not only ±1; adding the general
   helper avoids reimplementing branch resolution or partial validation
   in `src-tauri`. The existing ±1 API and its closed delta rule stay
   unchanged (`crates/eunomia-core/src/levels.rs:444-498`).
3. **`items_move(id, target)` names semantics, not stale positions.**
   The target is a tagged enum: `after_item { id }` (the original-list
   gap immediately after that row), `into_heading { id }` (the end of
   that heading's ALG-060 section), or `root` (the first root position).
   An instruction moved onto a heading lands at the section end; a
   heading branch moved onto a heading becomes its last child and calls
   the core helper with `target level + 1`; a branch moved to `root`
   calls it with level 2. A heading whose target heading lies inside its
   own ALG-060 branch is rejected before the move, including the
   otherwise boundary-shaped "drop a branch onto itself" case. Other
   interior gaps are rejected by the existing `move_branch`/`move_range`
   guard (`crates/eunomia-core/src/reorder.rs:277-320`). The dragged
   range is resolved ONCE on the pre-move list; automatic alignment is
   applied to that exact range before insertion, and the aligned range
   is then moved with `move_range`. Re-resolving the branch after
   insertion is incorrect: the old root level may close on an adjacent
   heading that the new, deeper root level would absorb (round-1 P1,
   pinned by the H4-target/H3-closer regression).
4. **The repository persists the core permutation.**
   `eunomia_store::library::set_item_order` validates that the supplied
   ids are exactly the current table-wide set, then writes every
   `position = index + 1` through one caller-owned transaction. The
   schema has no UNIQUE position index (`docs/spec.md:258-269`), so
   intermediate duplicates inside the transaction cannot violate a
   constraint; the final state is the DB-005/DB-011 dense sequence.
   The command never translates hierarchy into ad-hoc repeated
   `move_item` calls. Name validation is one linear core pass; each
   structure operation makes a linear number of linear store/core
   passes, with no text-processing loop nested inside another.
5. **Creation placement and history.** `heading_create(name, level,
parent)` appends at the table end when `parent` is absent (the
   header "+" root case), or at the end of the named heading's ALG-060
   branch when present (the row "+" child case). The caller supplies the
   level; the UI's level-6 disable remains UI policy. Heading create,
   rename, level change, branch shift, move and physical delete each
   write their existing `heading.*` journal action in the same
   transaction and write NO `revisions` row (§6.2's explicit heading
   exception, `docs/spec.md:346`). A moved heading branch is one
   `heading.changed` entry naming its root; a moved instruction is one
   `instruction.changed` entry. No-op moves journal nothing.
6. **Command count baseline verified, not guessed.** At this branch's
   base, `src-tauri/src/lib.rs:210-240` contains 29 registrations and
   `src/ipc/mode.spec.ts:24-54` pins the same 29 names. The brief's
   reported 30-vs-29 discrepancy is not present in this checkout; the
   existing machine-checked-count follow-up remains out of scope. This
   batch adds exactly four names, so the truthful registered count is 33.

Tests lead: all four absorbed DoDs get mock-IPC behavior tests over a
real migrated `Db`, with direct store/SQL read-back. The move suite
pins restart persistence, nested order (hidden items included), all

### D-190 — T-332: orphaned `.bak` copies get a read-only startup report and a manual rule instead of a silent cleanup — 2026-11-24

Problem: a `.bak` copy under `backups/` that no `backup_records` row
mentions has no owner. The backup retention (T-114) walks rows, the
phase-2 abort sweep (BKP-005) knows only its own run's copies, and
D-091 records how such a file appears: the copy is written straight
to its final §5.5 name, so a process death between the copy and its
record — or a record transaction that failed after the file was
verified — leaves verified bytes nothing points at. D-132's review
handed the debris over ("an owner for pre-existing orphan `.bak`
debris"), and the owner's triage of 2026-11-24 (option 2) ruled:
do not delete them silently — make them visible and fix the manual
rule of handling. No automatic cleanup at startup, no deferral.

Solution: a read-only report, `src-tauri/src/backup_orphans.rs`, run
once at the end of every successful `Db::open` — the same trigger as
the T-253 protective-copy pass, so every launch and every recovery
reopen reports, and both facts it needs (the data root and the open
connection) are already there. The pass reads **every**
`backup_records.backup_path` through the new
`eunomia_store::backup_records::all_paths` (all statuses: a `pruned`
or `discarded` row still claims the name it refers to) and lists
`backups/<project folder>/` one level deep; a `*.bak` file whose
relative layout string (`backups/<folder>/<file>`) is in no row's
cell is an orphan. Nothing is deleted, moved or rewritten. The cost
is one SELECT over the rows (the claim set is a `HashSet`, so its
construction and every lookup are expected-constant) plus two
directory levels of names — linear in rows plus entries, no file
opened, sized or hashed.

The ruling's three questions, answered in the line and in this
record:

- **What is shown.** One `warn` line
  (`logging::backup_orphans`) per run with numeric fields only —
  `orphan_files`, `orphan_folders` (folders holding at least one),
  `unreadable_folders` (folders the pass could not list, which makes
  the two counts a lower bound). No paths and no folder names: a
  folder name carries the project-name slug, i.e. stored user text
  (SEC-008). Two messages, never both: the orphan one when files
  were counted, and a distinct "the count is a lower bound" one when
  nothing was counted but a folder could not be listed (round-1
  review's P3-1: a zero from a partial pass must not read as a clean
  tree). A tree with no orphans and every folder readable logs
  nothing — the retention passes' no-op policy.
- **Who decides.** The user. The app never reclaims the space on its
  own: a copy with no row may be the only surviving evidence of a
  file (that is exactly the abort window D-091 records), so a silent
  sweep would destroy data the run was trying to protect.
- **What to do.** Inspect `<data dir>/backups/` and delete a file by
  hand when its content is not needed. There is no UI command for
  this in v1 (the backups screen and `backups_list` are T-125's);
  the log line is the whole report surface, and it repeats at every
  open while the files stay.

Degrade, never abort (the D-046/D-054 startup-housekeeping posture,
the T-253 pass's own contract): a failed records read
(`logging::backup_orphans_failed`) or an unlistable `backups/` root
(`logging::backup_orphans_unreadable`) logs and returns — the open
succeeds, and the next open retries the whole report. A project
folder that cannot be listed is not an error: it is counted in
`unreadable_folders` and the readable folders are still judged (the
protective copy pass's partially-unreadable posture). A missing
`backups/` root is the quiet answer, not an error. A non-UTF-8 entry
name fails the pass: a layout path is TEXT on the wire, so such a
name could never be claimed by a row and the counts could not be
trusted.

Tests: `backup_orphans.rs`'s inline module (twelve) — the
claimed/unclaimed pair (the only difference is the row's claim), a
root-level `.bak` and a non-`.bak` file, foreign files and a
directory squatting on a `.bak` name ignored, a non-UTF-8 entry name
failing the pass closed (Unix arm, skipping when the filesystem
refuses the bytes), folders counted once each, a missing root as the
quiet answer, the unreadable folder counted beside the readable ones
still judged (root-gated Unix arm, the availability suite's gate),
and five facade tests — four over a real migrated database with the
store's own writers, the root-unlistable one over an in-memory table
built for that arm alone: the orphan line with its counts and no
fragment of the fixture's user data (folder slug, project name and
label, source path, layout prefix), the claimed-only tree silent, the
unreadable-only pass on the lower-bound message (root-gated), a
dropped `backup_records` table on the records-read degrade line, and
a file squatting on `backups/` on the root-unlistable line. The store
side, `all_paths_returns_every_claimed_path_across_statuses` in
`tests/backup_records.rs`, pins the status-blind known set and the
empty-table answer. The wiring has its text pin in `db_tests.rs`
(`the_open_reports_orphaned_backup_copies_after_the_retention_pass`):
the call sits inside `Db::open`'s body, after the retention marker
and before the `Ok(Db { … })` tail, and a repo-wide census over the
crate's `src/*.rs` finds exactly one caller module (`db.rs`; the
needle is assembled at run time so the pin's own text cannot count).
Mutations run on the final tree, each restored byte-for-byte: the
`Db::open` call removed → the wiring pin red; a comment naming the
call dropped into another module → the census red; the claim test
inverted (`!known.contains` → true) → the counted-orphans tests red;
the missing-root arm removed → the quiet-answer test red; the
facade's branch flipped (`> 0` → `== 0`) → the orphan-line and
lower-bound tests red; `text_name` made lossy → the non-UTF-8 test
red.

Round-1 review (hy4-flash-free, report `.opencode/reviews/t332-r1.md`):
REQUEST CHANGES — 2×P2, 3×P3, all five taken in the amend. P2-1: the
architecture paragraph named `project_folders`; the emitted field is
`orphan_folders` (fixed there). P2-2: three documented branches had
no test — the non-UTF-8 fail-closed, a root-level `.bak` and the two
degrade lines — each gained its test (above). P3-1: "no orphans logs
nothing" was false for the unreadable-only pass, and "per session
start" contradicted the per-open trigger; the message split and the
wording are fixed. P3-2: the wiring pin now names the enclosing
function and the repo-wide census. P3-3: the SEC-008 assertion now
covers the fixture's real name, label and paths instead of a slug
that appears nowhere. The reviewer's note on complexity is answered
by the `HashSet` above.

Docs: ARCHITECTURE.md's open-path section gains the report's
paragraph beside the T-253 pass, and its module table the new file.
No spec change: §5.5/§7.6 pin the layout and the copies, not a
housekeeping report, and the requirement set has no row for it —
this is the owner's ruling, recorded here.

### D-192 — T-331: current custom-text ruling wins over the absorbed fork card; history and assignment contracts — 2026-11-24

Problem: T-331 repeats T-099's historical `variant_fork_for_project`
command and fork-a-variant acceptance criterion, but the current owner
ruling explicitly removed that command. D-125 A1 and its T-327 addendum
(`DECISIONS.md:10817-10834`, `:10922-10975`) replace it with
`assignment_set_custom`; the shipped schema still has only a non-null
`variant_id` (`crates/eunomia-store/migrations/0001_init.sql:125-134`),
and the current spec requires custom text in the assignment and in the
built body (`docs/spec.md:354-358`, `:476`, `:579-587`, `:601`, `:636`).
The card also leaves the history list's scope/order and the bulk wire
shape open.

Question: does T-331 implement the card's removed fork API, or the current
MAIN-007/LIB-018/S5 contract? Chosen reading: the later explicit owner
ruling and current spec win. T-331 lands `assignment_set_custom`, not the
removed `variant_fork_for_project`; it still adds exactly five commands.
T-099's observable goals are preserved without cloning variants: editing
one project never changes shared variant text, and a repeated edit updates
the same assignment instead of creating variants.

Solution — contracts and work plan chosen before implementation:

1. **Schema/store/core first.** Add forward-only migration 0003: direct
   instruction FK, nullable `variant_id`, nullable `custom_text`, and the
   exactly-one-target CHECK from spec §6.2. Existing rows copy verbatim.
   Store and core assignment targets are enums (`Variant` or `Custom`), so
   "both" and "neither" cannot be constructed in Rust; the database CHECK
   remains the independent floor. The rebuild keeps `foreign_keys=ON`: no
   table references `project_instructions`, so rename/copy/drop is safe in
   the one migration transaction, verified on populated v2 data by
   `schema_v3.rs` and `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` (D-030's v3 policy). The
   snapshot carries custom text and the body uses it (ALG-002/§9.2); deleting
   a variant moves only variant-backed assignments and never touches custom
   cells.
2. **History reads.** `revisions_list(instruction_id)` returns summary rows
   for the instruction's versions plus every variant's versions, including
   soft-deleted variants, newest first (`created_at DESC`, `rev_no DESC`,
   `id DESC` as a deterministic tie-break). The list carries id, entity
   type/id, rev_no, op, snapshot hash, reverted_from and created_at — time,
   operation and entity — but deliberately does not read or serialize the
   potentially large snapshot. `revision_get(id)` returns the one full row,
   including the canonical snapshot. Unknown instruction/heading ids and
   unknown/malformed revision rows are typed refusals/corruption, never
   guessed.
3. **Single assignment.** `assignment_set(project_id, instruction_id,
enabled, variant_id)` assigns an active same-instruction variant or the
   active main when `variant_id` is null on an unassigned cell; on an
   already-enabled custom cell, null is a no-op and only an explicit variant
   id converts it. Disabling removes the row. A same-target re-send writes
   and journals nothing. A real change writes
   one `assignment.changed` entry with `Details::Bulk { changed: 1 }` in
   the same transaction. No project file is opened or written.
4. **Bulk assignment.** `assignments_bulk(instruction_ids, project_ids,
enabled, variant_id)` forms the requested row/column product. A variant
   is legal only for one instruction; null selects each instruction's
   main. Duplicate input ids collapse before work. Every already-present
   pair (including a custom cell) is left untouched and returned in
   `already_assigned`; other pairs are applied in ONE transaction and one
   `assignment.changed` entry carries the changed count. A bulk entry has no
   synthetic single-entity id; its count is the object summary. Any refusal
   rolls back the whole product. Processing is linear in the number of
   unique requested pairs plus the active-variant scan (when no variant is
   supplied) and validated text length, with indexed per-pair store
   reads/writes; the 100-assignment test is the scale pin.
5. **Per-project custom text.** `assignment_set_custom(project_id,
instruction_id, content)` validates §6.9 text before DB resolution.
   `Some(text)` upserts a custom-target assignment (empty text is legal);
   `None` replaces an existing custom target with the instruction's active
   main and is a no-op for an absent or variant-backed cell. Same-text
   re-sends write/journal nothing. No revision is created because the
   assignment is not a versioned library entity.
6. **Tests lead each layer.** Red-first migration/store/core tests, then
   mock-IPC command tests for all four absorbed DoDs, rollback, validation,
   idempotence, file non-modification and the 100-pair batch; finally mock
   frontend twins and binding regeneration. Every new test gets a
   behavior-changing mutation check. Documentation, the 38-command count,
   `mode.spec`, manual smoke, full checks and two model reviews follow.

Baseline before edits: `cargo nextest run --workspace --test-threads=4`
1787/1787 and `pnpm test` 345/345, both exit 0. No dependency or unsafe
addition is needed.

**Landing addendum (same task, 2026-11-24).** The chosen contracts are
implemented: migration 0003 and the store/core assignment-target enums;
`src-tauri/src/assignments.rs` and `revisions.rs` with five registered
commands, DTOs, error mappers and logging edges; regenerated bindings; and
frontend mock twins over mutable assignment/history rows. The history wire
uses decimal strings for SQLite's i64 `rev_no`/`reverted_from`: tauri-specta
forbids BigInt-style Rust integers, and narrowing them to JavaScript numbers
would lose precision. `ProjectLabelEntry.variant_id` is nullable so a custom
cell still labels its project without inventing a variant id.

Thirty-six new tests lead the behavior: 28 Rust (2 core custom-text tests plus
one strengthened target-serialization test, 2 schema v3, 4 store assignment, 2
store history, 13 assignment mock-IPC, 4 revision mock-IPC, and 1 custom-label
`library_get` test) and 8 frontend mock tests. The 100-pair DoD is one call from
an empty world, not two calls whose totals add to 100. History list assertions
include a raw-wire check that no `snapshot` field is serialized.

Mutation battery: 39 behavior-changing mutants, 39 killed in one retained run;
every source file was restored byte-for-byte and SHA-256 checked after each
mutant. The battery covers target tagging, custom text and empty-custom builds,
migration copy and CHECK floors, store no-op/clear/delete/reassign/decode scope,
history order/corruption, main default, bulk count/dedupe/error rollback/
custom-cell skip/journal entity, custom validation/content/journal/enable
semantics, single no-op/journal, sync and no-database gates, registration,
custom labels and the frontend twins. The final evidence is
`.opencode/reviews/t331_mutations-20261124T183031905440.jsonl`; invocation logs
are timestamp-suffixed rather than truncated, so reruns cannot erase prior

### D-195 — CI 45542135360: local-green/CI-red — doctests outside the nextest gate, and a microsecond clock colliding temp-dir labels — 2026-11-24

Problem: CI run 45542135360 (main, `3c1c5e4..748c7de`, T-331 on top)
was red on every test-matrix leg while the local suite on the same tree
was 1831/1831 green. Two independent defects, both introduced by
T-331's `748c7de`:

1. All four legs failed the `Rust tests` step at the same doc-test: the
   `BuildSnapshot` example (`crates/eunomia-core/src/snapshot.rs:190`)
   used `AssignmentTarget` at :232 but its import list at :193 named only
   `Assignment` — `E0433`, the example cannot compile. CI runs
   `cargo test --workspace` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:192`), which
   compiles doc-tests; the local gate runs `cargo nextest run
--workspace`, and nextest executes no doc-tests (clippy's
   `--all-targets` compiles none either), so a deterministic compile
   break reached main invisible to every local check — D-192's rebase
   check list shows exactly that hole.
2. macos-15-intel alone failed both tests of
   `crates/eunomia-store/tests/schema_v3.rs` with SQLite errors.
   `v3_rejects…` at :173 got `Migration` wrapping "table settings
   already exists"; `v2_assignments…` at :114 got `Backup` wrapping
   "disk I/O error" from `VACUUM INTO` (`storage.rs:843`). Root cause:
   both tests built their scratch directory with the same
   `temp_dir("upgrade")` label (748c7de's :107/:171). The name is label
   plus pid plus `SystemTime::now()` nanos, and that runner's clock is
   microsecond-fine — the collided path's nanos (`…625143000`) is a
   whole microsecond — so the two parallel-spawned tests read one tick
   and shared one directory and one `db.sqlite3`: test 2 read
   `user_version = 0` before test 1's seed transaction committed, then
   its `CREATE TABLE settings` ran after the commit (a deferred write
   transaction applies to the latest committed state) → "table settings
   already exists"; test 2's panic ran `TempDir::drop` → `remove_dir_all`
   on the shared directory under test 1's in-flight `VACUUM INTO` →
   "disk I/O error". One cause, both messages — and cargo's fail-fast
   masked that leg's doc-test failure (schema_v3 runs before the
   doc-tests).

Solution (the CI-fix service commit, referencing T-331):

1. The example now imports both types:
   `use eunomia_core::assignment::{Assignment, AssignmentTarget};` —
   the shape of `assignment.rs`'s own example. Reproduced red locally
   with `cargo test --doc --workspace`, green after the fix
   (eunomia-core 86, eunomia-fs 12, the other crates 0 — no further
   hidden doc-test failures).
2. The second test's label is now `"rejects"`; distinct labels make the
   two directories disjoint by construction — the invariant every
   sibling suite already keeps (a repo-wide audit of all
   `temp_dir`/`temp_data_dir` call sites found the duplicate only in
   `schema_v3.rs`). The helper now documents the uniqueness contract.
3. Ruling: a task that touches Rust adds `cargo test --doc --workspace`
   to its check chain — nextest alone cannot see doc-tests, and CI's
   `cargo test --workspace` keeps catching what the local gate misses.
   The scheme's residual exposure (a future same-label pair plus one
   clock tick) stays open as a board follow-up: a shared helper or a
   per-process counter would close the class, not the instance.
